stances.claim: Compulsory infrastructure access under a 'necessary' standard is a radical departure from the globally accepted indispensability test, which requires dominance, non-replicability, and refusal that would eliminate competition.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-deviation argument against the access threshold

stances.claim: Forcing telcos to open privately built infrastructure to competitors without negotiation or market-based compensation amounts to a regulatory taking that is 'simply unconscionable.'
The KP impliedly amends the Philippine Competition Act and redistributes regulatory roles without clear legislative notice, violating the one-subject-one-title rule.
Section 5(e)'s grant to DICT to define 'other segments' of digital infrastructure lacks sufficient standards and runs afoul of the nondelegation doctrine.
Splitting regulatory authority among DICT, DEPDev, PCC, and the traditional NTC produces vague lines of authority that risk delays, overlap, and diluted accountability.
The transitory clause limiting legislative franchises to non-data services violates due process and the non-impairment of contracts by modifying property-like rights midstream.
The Constitution does not hinder progress -- it is the very structure through which reforms gain legitimacy.

notable_anecdotes: The author's use of Southern Luzon Drug Corp. v. DSWD (April 25, 2017) to anchor the principle that regulatory taking does not always require physical appropriation but occurs when a party is substantially deprived of beneficial use or value of its property.

The KP transitory clause stating legislative franchises 'shall remain valid only to the extent they do not involve data transmission' -- flagged as midstream modification of franchise rights upon which infrastructure financing was planned.
The contrast between a 'necessary' access test (KP) and the global 'indispensability' essential-facilities test (dominance + non-replicability + refusal eliminating competition).

one_paragraph_summary: In Part 2 of his Konektadong Pinoy critique, Panganiban takes up three further constitutional defects. On infrastructure access, he argues that Sections 7, 12, and 13 -- requiring PTEs to grant access to registered DTIPs whenever 'necessary' to compete, and mandating a Reference Access Offer that eliminates negotiation -- radically depart from the global 'indispensability' test under the essential facilities doctrine (dominance, non-replicability, refusal eliminating competition), and risk regulatory taking under Article III, Section 9, citing Southern Luzon Drug Corp. v. DSWD (April 25, 2017) for the rule that substantial deprivation of beneficial use suffices. He also flags implied amendments to the Philippine Competition Act that violate Article VI, Section 26(1)'s one-subject-one-title rule. On delegation, Section 5(e)'s grant to DICT to define 'other segments' of digital infrastructure lacks sufficient standards under the nondelegation doctrine, and the redistribution of regulatory roles among DICT, the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development, the Philippine Competition Commission, and the traditional NTC produces vague lines of authority that risk delays, overlap, and diluted accountability. On private property, the transitory clause limiting legislative franchises to non-data services modifies franchise rights midstream and violates due process and the non-impairment of contracts, undermining investor confidence and long-term infrastructure planning. He closes -- as in Part 1 -- by reaffirming support for the KP's noble aims of access, competition, and innovation, but insists that reforms must remain within constitutional bounds because the Constitution is not a hindrance but the very structure through which reforms gain legitimacy.
